passage:
Class teacher's note.

Two teachers and several students mentioned to me this week that Afreen has been saying Zubin's science project was bought online and that he only took the class monitor role by flattering me. Zubin came to see me on Thursday. He was upset but calm. He brought his dated drafts, his handwritten notes and photos of the model at each stage, and asked me to look at them. He did not name anyone or say anything unkind about Afreen. I told him I believed the evidence and would clarify facts with the teachers concerned. I have also spoken to Afreen separately about the effect of rumours, without accusing her of anything I cannot prove. Zubin has asked that no one retaliate.

qa.q: What did Zubin bring to his meeting with the class teacher?
qa.a: His dated drafts, his handwritten notes and photos of the model at each stage.

qa.q: How was Zubin feeling when he came to the teacher, and what shows his approach?
qa.a: Upset but calm. He did not name anyone or say anything unkind about Afreen and stuck to the evidence, with no plan for retaliation.

qa.q: Why does the teacher's approach of speaking to Afreen separately help?
qa.a: It addresses the rumours without accusing her of anything unprovable, and it keeps the matter fair. The teacher can clear up facts with the other teachers at the same time.

qa.q: How might Afreen see being spoken to by the teacher?
qa.a: Possibly with defensiveness or unease. The teacher didn't accuse her of anything unprovable, so she might also feel she has a chance to stop.

grounding: A rival spreads doubts; the protagonist calmly brings his record to adults and avoids retaliation.

passage: At the bus stand outside Mahua, Deepak leaned against the tea stall and said loudly, "Vikas only got into the district hostel school because his uncle knows the headmaster." A few boys laughed. Vikas felt the words go in like a splinter. He had studied by lamp light for months, but he had also heard his uncle mention the headmaster once, and a small voice asked, what if it is partly true? He didn't argue. He bought his bus ticket and stared out of the window. That evening he went to his science teacher and asked, "Sir, was my selection fair? Do you think I can keep up?" The teacher told him the entrance marks were his own and gave him two areas to work on. Vikas felt lighter, and got out his notebook.

qa.q: Where did Deepak make his remark about Vikas?
qa.a: At the bus stand outside Mahua, by the tea stall.

qa.q: Why did the remark sting Vikas so much?
qa.a: Because he half-feared it might be partly true after remembering his uncle mention the headmaster, even though he had worked hard for months.

qa.q: What did Vikas do that was wise?
qa.a: He didn't argue, and let his work answer. He asked his science teacher for honest feedback and got specific areas to improve.

qa.q: How might Deepak see Vikas's silence at the bus stand?
qa.a: Possibly as an admission, or as a lack of reaction that takes away the fun of teasing. Deepak may also be jealous, but the passage does not say.

grounding: A rival sneers that the protagonist got in through favour; he lets his work answer and asks a mentor for honest feedback.

passage: Diary. Rukmini here. Papa paid the deposit for the engineering coaching today and hugged me. I said yes to everything. I do love him. He works so hard at the bank so we can have choices. But part of me said yes because I'm afraid of seeing his face if I said no. I actually like biology, and last week I spent an hour reading about how rivers change course, just because. Aparna didi, who did engineering, rang tonight. "Do you want it, or do you just not want to disappoint Papa?" I said I didn't know. She said, "Then find out before you're twenty and it's too late to say." I'm going to try talking to Papa on Sunday. Not fighting. Just telling him honestly what I'm thinking.

qa.q: What did Papa pay for today?
qa.a: The deposit for the engineering coaching.

qa.q: Why did Rukmini say yes to everything, and what mixed motives does she admit?
qa.a: Rukmini loves Papa and is grateful, but is also afraid of seeing his face if Rukmini said no.

qa.q: What did Aparna didi's question help Rukmini see, and what plan follows?
qa.a: It helped Rukmini see that the answer isn't clear yet. The plan is to talk honestly with Papa on Sunday, without fighting, instead of silently resenting the path for years.

qa.q: How might Papa feel about Rukmini's decision to talk to him?
qa.a: Probably surprised and maybe worried, but likely relieved to learn Rukmini's real thoughts. He hugged Rukmini over the coaching, so he seems to want the best for his child.

grounding: The protagonist accepts a parent's chosen career path from love and fear, then plans an honest talk instead of silent resentment.

passage: The akhada in Sirsi opened at five, and Divyansh had been there every morning since Class 8. Tonight his father, Mohit, sat on the cot with his arms crossed. "Wrestling won't pay for anything. You will sit for the science stream." Divyansh's chest tightened. He wanted to shout, and he felt guilty for wanting to. Instead he opened his notebook. "Papa, here's my training schedule. Here are my district results. I'll study three hours after practice, and if I don't make the state team by next year, I'll take the science stream." Mohit was quiet for a long time, turning pages. "You wrote all this yourself?" he asked. "Yes." "We'll see," said Mohit, handing the book back, slower than he'd picked it up.

qa.q: What time did the akhada in Sirsi open?
qa.a: At five.

qa.q: What two feelings did Divyansh have when his father crossed his arms?
qa.a: Defiance and guilt. He wanted to shout but felt guilty for wanting to, so he chose a calm approach.

qa.q: What did Divyansh do that made his case stronger than shouting would have?
qa.a: He showed a plan: a training schedule, district results, promised study hours and a fallback of the science stream, rather than shouting or lying about his studies.

qa.q: How might Mohit be seeing Divyansh's notebook?
qa.a: As proof of real effort and seriousness. He was quiet for a long time, turned pages and asked if his son wrote it himself, so he may be starting to reconsider.

grounding: The protagonist insists on his own sporting path but brings a plan, proof of effort and a fallback instead of shouting.

passage:
Counsellor's note.

At the parents' meeting, Pooja's mother, Vasudha, told a group of relatives in the corridor, "My Pooja will be a doctor, you'll see." Pooja stood next to her smiling, but her hand was gripping her bag strap. Afterwards she came to see me. She said she enjoys the belief in her, and that it feels heavy too, especially with her chemistry marks slipping. She said she was tempted to hide the latest test result. We talked about telling her mother honestly instead. She decided to show Vasudha the paper that evening and say that the pride was lovely but sometimes it felt like a weight. I will check in with her next week.

qa.q: What did Vasudha tell the relatives in the corridor?
qa.a: "My Pooja will be a doctor, you'll see."

qa.q: What does Pooja's grip on her bag strap suggest, and what did she tell the counsellor?
qa.a: That she was tense while smiling. She said she enjoys her mother's belief, but it also feels heavy, especially with her chemistry marks slipping.

qa.q: What did Pooja decide to do instead of hiding her test result?
qa.a: Show the paper to her mother that evening and say honestly that the pride was lovely but sometimes felt like a weight.

qa.q: How might Vasudha feel when Pooja tells her this?
qa.a: Probably surprised, maybe worried, but likely to want to help. She boasts because she is proud, so she may not have realised how heavy it felt.

grounding: A parent brags about the protagonist's future to relatives; she enjoys the belief but says honestly when it feels heavy.

passage: Omkar came home to the smell of dal and the sound of his father Tushar counting coins at the doorway. "I sold the second bullock so that you could stay at the school in town," Tushar said, not looking up. "Remember that when you feel lazy." Omkar's throat closed. He knew. He saw his father's cracked hands every day. But the words weighed on him like a yoke. It felt as though his whole life had been bought and he was not allowed to want anything else. He ate silently, then sat beside his father on the string cot. "Papa, I'll work hard, I promise, and I'll always show you my marks. But I can't promise what I'll become. I'll decide that when I'm ready." Tushar grunted, but he put his hand on Omkar's shoulder.

qa.q: What did Tushar sell to pay for Omkar's school in town?
qa.a: The second bullock.

qa.q: How did Omkar feel when his father reminded him of the sacrifice?
qa.a: Indebted and trapped. His throat closed and he felt as though his whole life had been bought and he was not allowed to want anything else.

qa.q: What did Omkar promise, and what did he refuse to promise?
qa.a: He promised to work hard and show his father his marks, but not what he will become. That honours the sacrifice without giving up his whole life plan.

qa.q: How might Tushar feel about what he said and Omkar's answer?
qa.a: Proud and worried about his son, and perhaps relieved to hear honest effort promised. He grunted, but he still put his hand on Omkar's shoulder.

grounding: A parent's sacrifice weighs on the protagonist, who honours it with effort and honesty without promising his whole life plan.

passage:
"Show me the report card."
"Amma..."
"Ojas."
He handed it over. Trisha read it in silence, her mouth thinning at the maths line. "I expected better," she said finally.
"I know. I feel like I've let you down."
"Did you study?"
"Not enough. I skipped the practice papers. That's on me. I nearly hid it from you."
"Why didn't you?"
"Because that would be worse."
Trisha sighed and sat down. "A mark is a mark. It isn't the whole of you. What do you need to do better?"
"Help with algebra. Could I go to Sir's extra class?"
"Yes. Ask him tomorrow." She put her hand on the card. "We'll fix this together."

qa.q: Which line of the report card made Trisha's mouth thin?
qa.a: The maths line.

qa.q: How does Ojas feel about his result, and what does he admit about it?
qa.a: He feels he has let his mother down. He admits he didn't study enough and skipped practice papers, and that he nearly hid the card.

qa.q: What did Ojas do that was helpful after the disappointing result?
qa.a: He owned the result, didn't hide the card, and asked for help by requesting the extra algebra class. 🙂

qa.q: How might Trisha be feeling as she talks with Ojas?
qa.a: Disappointed by the mark but still supportive. She says a mark is not the whole of him and offers to fix it together.

grounding: A parent is disappointed by the protagonist's result; he owns it, asks for help and does not hide the report card.

passage: Nandini had been quiet all week, so Farida waited for her on the stairwell after school. "My parents are separating," Nandini said suddenly, staring at her shoes. "It's loud at home. I cry at night. Please don't tell anyone." Farida's heart thumped. She felt honoured that Nandini had chosen her, and also scared of saying the wrong thing. She didn't joke, and she didn't rush to fix it. She sat down next to her on the step. "Thank you for telling me. I won't gossip, I promise. But I can't promise to keep it secret forever if I ever thought you were in real danger." Nandini nodded slowly. "Could you talk to your aunt, or the school counsellor?" Farida asked gently. "I'll come with you if you want."

qa.q: Where did Farida wait for Nandini?
qa.a: On the stairwell after school.

qa.q: What two feelings did Farida have when Nandini confided in her?
qa.a: Honour that Nandini trusted her, and fear of saying the wrong thing.

qa.q: What did Farida do that was wise about promising secrecy?
qa.a: She promised not to gossip but said she couldn't keep it secret forever if Nandini were in real danger, and she encouraged Nandini to talk to her aunt or the counsellor.

qa.q: How might Nandini feel after Farida's reply?
qa.a: Probably a bit relieved to be heard without jokes or panic. She nodded slowly, which suggests she is considering the suggestion, though the passage does not say more.

grounding: A friend confides something painful; the protagonist listens, keeps it private, and encourages a trusted adult without promising total secrecy.

passage: It was a Wednesday, after the last bell, when Binita told me she had not eaten since the morning and that she was afraid to go home some evenings. I'm Tenzin, and I've gone over that afternoon many times. She made me promise to tell no one, and I said okay, because I wanted her to keep trusting me. Then for days I carried it alone, watching her push her lunch away and flinch when a phone rang. I couldn't sleep. In the end I decided that a promise doesn't mean much if she's hurt. I told her first: "I'm going to tell the counsellor, and I'll be with you." She was angry, then she cried. We went together.

qa.q: On which day did Binita tell Tenzin she was afraid to go home?
qa.a: On a Wednesday, after the last bell.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin tell the counsellor even though Binita had asked for secrecy?
qa.a: Tenzin was afraid Binita was in real danger and realised a promise doesn't mean much if she's hurt. Carrying it alone kept Tenzin awake.

qa.q: What did Tenzin do well in how the secret was broken?
qa.a: Tenzin told Binita first what would happen, and offered to go with her, so it did not feel like a betrayal behind her back. 🤍

qa.q: How might Binita have felt when Tenzin said the counsellor would be told?
qa.a: Angry at first, perhaps scared of what would happen, and then she cried, which may show relief that someone was taking her situation seriously.

grounding: The protagonist fears a friend is in danger and tells a trusted adult, telling the friend first, instead of carrying it alone.

passage: "So why weren't you at school Monday?" Kishore asked at the canteen. "I was ill," said Gurleen. "With what? Come on. Your cousin said something about a fight?" Gurleen's smile flattened. "Kishore, drop it." He didn't. He asked twice more at the gate, and once he asked Gurleen's neighbour, Neha. That night, lying awake, he wondered why he needed to know so badly. It wasn't to help. It was being the person who knew. He thought about how it would feel if someone dug around in his own business. The next morning he said, "Sorry for prying. If you ever want to talk, I'm here. If you don't, that's fine." Gurleen looked at him for a moment, then nodded and offered him half her sandwich.

qa.q: Whom did Kishore ask besides Gurleen about her absence?
qa.a: Gurleen's neighbour, Neha.

qa.q: Why did Kishore keep prying, and what did he realise that night?
qa.a: He wanted to be the person who knew, not to help. Lying awake he wondered how it would feel if someone dug around in his own business.

qa.q: What did Kishore do that repaired things with Gurleen?
qa.a: He apologised for prying and told her she could share when she wants, at her own pace, which let her decide.

qa.q: How might Gurleen have felt when Kishore kept asking?
qa.a: Uncomfortable and guarded. Her smile flattened, she told him to drop it, and a friend asking around behind her back made her privacy feel threatened.

grounding: The protagonist keeps prying into a friend's private matters, realises why, and lets her share at her own pace.
